title: Partially Correlated Verifier Cascades: Concave Log-Odds and Blind-Spot Ceilings
hook: Chain enough independent verifier checks and failure should vanish exponentially. In practice, treating correlated verifiers as independent underestimates failure by 20x at 5 checks — and 3000x at 10.
key_points: Studies serial verification gates — an answer passes only if k verifier calls all accept it — under realistic, correlated (not independent) failure rates.
Models the per-instance false-accept rate as a latent variable; the exact posterior shows log-odds are concave in k, with the prior 'Odds Law' (independent case) as just its tangent upper bound.
For Beta-distributed latents, failure decays polynomially in k rather than exponentially, with a correlation parameter identifiable from just two repeated verdicts per instance.
A 'blind-spot' mass of instances that always false-accept caps how much reliability any number of gates can buy — failure saturates above zero no matter how many checks you add.
Whether adding more gates helps, plateaus, or actively hurts depends on the tails of the underlying latent distributions, with a closed-form crossover point.

In synthetic tests, assuming independence underestimates real failure by about 20x at 5 gates and about 3000x at 10 gates; the practical fix is decorrelating verifiers (different model family, modality, or evidence source), not stacking more of them.
content_html: Chaining independent verifier checks is a common reliability trick in LLM harnesses: only accept an answer if k separate verifier calls all agree. Under conditional independence, a recent result (the "Odds Law") showed failure decays exponentially in k — but real verifier gates are rarely independent, and the theory explicitly left "a tight theory of partially correlated verifier cascades" as an open problem.
extra_html:
Jiangang Han supplies that theory. Modeling each instance's false-accept rate as a latent variable drawn from a distribution G, the exact cascade posterior turns out to be concave in k — the Odds Law is just its tangent line at the first gate, and an upper bound rather than the truth. For Beta-distributed latents, failure decays only polynomially in k, with a correlation parameter that two repeated verdicts per instance are enough to identify. A further "blind-spot" mass of instances that always false-accept caps how much reliability any number of gates can buy, so failure saturates above zero rather than vanishing. Letting the true-accept rate vary too produces a trichotomy: depending on the tails of the underlying distributions, adding more gates can help forever, plateau, or actively make things worse, with a closed-form crossover point marking which regime you're in.

The gap between the tidy independent theory and reality is large: in synthetic tests, assuming independence underestimates real failure by about 20x at 5 gates and roughly 3000x at 10 gates, while a correlated fit using repeated verdicts tracks held-out results accurately. The practical takeaway is that piling on more correlated gates has diminishing (or negative) returns — the real lever is decorrelation, changing the model family, modality, or evidence source behind each check. Jiangang Han, arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

flashcards.prompt: What assumption does the earlier 'Odds Law' make about verifier gates, and why does it break down in practice?
flashcards.back_html: It assumes verifier gates are conditionally independent, so log-odds of success grow linearly in the number of gates k. Real gates are correlated — errors that survive one gate tend to be the kind that survive others too.

flashcards.prompt: How badly does assuming independence underestimate real cascade failure, per the paper's synthetic tests?

choices.text: About 20x at 5 gates, and about 3000x at 10 gates
About 2x at any number of gates
It doesn't underestimate — independence is a safe approximation

flashcards.explanation_html: The gap grows fast with more gates: roughly 20x underestimation at k=5 and roughly 3000x at k=10, because correlated failures don't keep shrinking exponentially the way independent ones would.

flashcards.prompt: What is the paper's recommended fix for verifier cascades that stop improving with more gates?

choices.text: Decorrelate the verifiers — e.g. use a different model family, modality, or evidence source — rather than just adding more gates
Add as many additional identical gates as computationally possible
Switch to a single, very large verifier model instead of a cascade

flashcards.explanation_html: A 'blind-spot' of instances that always false-accept caps how much reliability more identical gates can buy; the practical lever is decorrelation, not gate count.
